articles.title: Republican inadvertently calls Trump's biggest success the 'scandal of my lifetime'
articles.description: A GOP senator accidentally called President Donald Trump's biggest success the "scandal of my lifetime" with his comments on Fox News. Sen. Ron Johnson spoke with Fox News on Wednesday about COVID vaccinations in light of the recent testimony by Anthony Fauci. He told anchor Laura Ingraham that "these injections cause death" and that the COVID vaccine is the "great government scandal of my lifetime." However, online critics noted that Trump boasted in the past that his first administration rolled out the COVID vaccines and that Johnson's comments amounted to calling Trump's success a scandal. "Trump literally said, 'I came up with the vaccines,'" progressive news personality Alex Cole wrote in a post on X. "If you believe Ron Johnson, then isn't he admitting Trump's biggest accomplishment was a disaster?" Democratic strategist Leslie Marshall similarly noted that Johnson was slamming COVID vaccines that "Trump green-lighted expeditiously." "He is a really dangerous liar. Who is he working for??" legal analyst Sara Dillon posted , mocking Johnson's attack on Fauci, who worked for the Trump administration during COVID. Others simply went after Ron Johnson's claims that COVID vaccines "cause death." "Ron Johnson needs a warning label," blogger Jim Stewartson wrote . "Having him on television is a risk to public health, an act of deadly negligence. FOX should be sued by everyone who lost someone because they listened to compromised idiots like this." "This isn't just political posturing: this is evil and will hurt innocent people," lawyer and political commentator John Jackson posted . "It's not enough to beat the Republican Party. We need to expose them so badly that they have to change their name."

articles.title: From bad to worse for Trump and his base
Democratic state lawmakers push to hold ICE accountable nationwide
articles.description:
A group of Democratic state lawmakers from around the nation were in Chicago Wednesday to push for more legislation that would give the public the ability to sue ICE agents over fatal shootings and arrests made without warrants.

“I never imagined that I would spend the majority of my first two years in my term drafting laws and helping support laws that protect people from our own federal government,” said state Sen. Graciela Guzman (D-Chicago) who led a news conference organized by an advocacy group known as State Innovation Exchange.

“I thought we'd be talking about lowering healthcare, lowering costs, funding our schools, and fighting for a more equitable Illinois. Instead, this (Trump) administration has forced states like ours into a different kind of work, which is defending our communities from federal overreach.”

Last fall, Illinois became among the few states in the country to allow residents to sue immigration agents who violate their constitutional rights to due process and protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.

House Bill 1312 was signed into law last fall. The law’s other key provision bans civil immigration arrests in and around Illinois courthouses.

Lawmakers from other states, including Georgia, Maryland, Utah, Colorado and Minnesota, said they also are pushing for protections for their residents.

“We have had federal agents break car windows and rain glass down on one-year-old children, or throw middle-aged women to the ground who were peacefully protesting,” said Colorado state Sen. Mike Weissman. “All of us up here are state legislators who deeply believe in using the power that we have under our constitution as states to simply try to make life more livable and more dignified for our constituents.”

The shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota in January and now the targeting of immigrants with expired visas at U.S. airports are examples why state lawmakers have to move fast with legislation, said Minnesota state Sen. Omar Fateh.

Feteh, whose district is on the south side of Minneapolis, said he authored legislation in early 2024 to protect Minnesotans from the violation of their rights by immigration agents. But, he said his fellow lawmakers felt it was too soon, too politically risky and too hypothetical to pass.

“Beginning in late 2025, Trump sent 3,000 armed, masked, untrained agents to Minnesota. It was the largest federal invasion in American history in a state that has less than 1% of the nation's undocumented people. Trump's agents rounded up random people on the street, they arrested whole families, young children, moms, and old women," Feteh said.

"They pursued, harassed, detained, arrested, and jailed Minnesotans in every stage of immigration, including legal status, refugees, naturalized citizens, even second and third generation citizens, and then they killed two civilian observers, Renee Good and Alex Pretti,” Feteh added. “Suddenly, the fight to protect people from Trump's fascism went from being too early to seemingly too late."

Guzman, co-chair of the Illinois Latino Legislative Caucus, said five lawsuits have been filed under the new state law.

Michael Puente is a reporter and anchor for WBEZ. Reach him mpuente@wbez.org.

articles.title: Trump slights 'clearly terrified' Supreme Court justice in wild Truth Social post
articles.description: President Donald Trump appeared to endorse a theory that Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett – whom he nominated in 2020 – is "clearly terrified of the left," sharing a prominent right-wing figure's post about her voting record on social media Wednesday. Conservative podcaster Tim Pool wrote that "Amy Coney Barrett is clearly terrified of the left" in response to a viral post on X highlighting her voting record and a supposed drop-off in her alignment with the bench's other conservative justices . Trump shared Pool’s post on his social media platform Truth Social without additional commentary. The apparent slight represents the latest example of Trump’s growing hostility toward the Supreme Court, including toward justices he nominated. While the Supreme Court has handed Trump an unprecedented amount of judicial victories , it's also handed down several notable defeats to his agenda, rejecting his bid to appeal a civil defamation case and ruling against most of his so-called reciprocal tariffs. The viral post Pool was responding to was authored by an anonymous right-wing account known as 'Roscoe Smith IV,' which claimed that Barrett’s rate of voting with the “conservative position” in “non-unanimous cases” fell from 81% “into the 50-60% range” following the court’s decision on Dobbs v. Jackson . The claim, however, was found inaccurate by X’s automatic fact-checking service known as “community notes,” which flagged publicly available data suggesting Barrett has voted alongside conservative justices at rates higher than the viral post suggested.

articles.title: Why Anthony Fauci might not be safe after pleading the Fifth
Fed leaves rates steady, with internal dissent
articles.description: The Federal Reserve left its interest rate target unchanged Wednesday amid significant internal dissent from officials who preferred to raise rates. The big picture: The central bank elected not to surprise markets with an interest rate hike, contrary to rampant speculation on Wall Street in recent days. But three members of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee did favor raising the cost of borrowing. Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed president Neel Kashkari, and Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan preferred a quarter-point rate hike, with the other nine officials, including chairman Kevin Warsh, voting to stand pat. Driving the news: The committee left its target range for the federal funds rate between 3.5% and 3.75%, where it has stood since December. "Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East," said the post-meeting policy statement, repeating language from the June meeting. Indeed, the statement was virtually unchanged from the last meeting, offering no clues as to whether or in what circumstances the committee might raise rates later this year. State of play: While most Fed watchers anticipated the holding action and financial markets priced it in as the most likely result of the meeting, there were rumblings in the last 10 days that persistently high inflation combined with a resurgence in energy prices might prompt a rate hike. Before the meeting, markets put the odds at roughly 1 in 3 on that outcome, the most uncertainty around a Fed rate decision in years. Warsh, in his second meeting at the helm, has eschewed the kind of clear guidance about future rate moves that his predecessors tended to use — instead favoring that policy meetings feature a "good family fight," where the outcome isn't pre-ordained. By the numbers: The Commerce Department releases June income and spending data Thursday. Analysts expect that it will show the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the Fed's go-to inflation gauge, was up 3.7% over the last 12 months. It has been above the Fed's 2% target every month since March 2021. Fed officials have chalked up a recent resurgence to one-off events like new tariffs and the Iran war, but several are losing patience and worry that the central bank's credibility as an inflation fighter is undermined by the sustained high inflation. "The Committee will deliver price stability," the statement said, repeating June language. What's next: Warsh will take questions from the news media in a press conference at 2:30pm ET.

articles.title: Fauci takes Fifth Amendment, refuses to answer Senate panel questions
articles.description: Dr. Anthony Fauci, who led the nation's infectious disease efforts during the pandemic, invoked the Fifth Amendment on Wednesday and declined to answer questions from a Senate committee investigating the origins of COVID-19. Why it matters: Fauci said Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), the head of the Senate homeland security committee, was trying to get him to say something that could put him in legal jeopardy. Former President Biden gave Fauci a preemptive pardon before leaving office, but Fauci argues he could be in trouble if he makes any statements that could open new lines of investigation for the committee. What he's saying: Paul has an "unhinged obsession with me," and his motive for the hearing is to "get me to say something — anything — that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, behind bars unquote," Fauci said. "Although it pains me to do so ... under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci said. The other side: "There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today," Paul told Fauci. This is breaking news. Check back for updates.

articles.title: Situation in Middle East comes under discussion as DPM Dar meets Kuwait FM
articles.description: The situation in the Middle East came under discussion as Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar on Wednesday met Kuwait’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, who is on an official visit to the country. According to the Foreign Office (FO), the two held a “warm and productive” tête-à-tête at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. “The two leaders reviewed the full spectrum of Pakistan–Kuwait bilateral relations and reaffirmed their shared commitment to further strengthening the longstanding brotherly partnership,” it said. “They also held in-depth discussions on regional and international developments, with particular focus on the evolving situation in the Middle East,” it added. The visiting dignitary arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday at the invitation of Deputy PM Dar. The FO said that upon arrival at the Islamabad International Airport, he was received by Zahid Hussain, additional secretary at the foreign ministry. It added that the minister’s visit to Pakistan reflected the longstanding brotherly relations between the two countries, “anchored in shared history, mutual trust and close cooperation”. Announcing the visit on Monday, the FO said Kuwait’s top diplomat was expected to pay a courtesy call on the leadership of Pakistan. Pakistan has been negotiating an expanded defence pact with Kuwait in exchange for energy cooperation and investment, the Reuters news agency reported earlier this month, citing five sources with knowledge of the talks.
